content_list.content_text: In the early years of silent film, African Americans were not portrayed in a positive light. Their characters were limited to highly stereotyped roles and, more often than not, if an African American appeared in a film, the role would be played by a white actor wearing blackface. But men like Noble Johnson (1881-1978) and Oscar Micheaux (1884-1951) were not content to simply stand by, watching sequel after sequel of these blatantly racist depictions. They knew there were many African American actors and actresses who were capable of acting if they were given a chance.

Even knowing it would be hard work, these men were willing to take the risk. These film pioneers would begin producing films with all-Black casts aimed at the African American community. These films, which came to be called black race films, or simply Race Films, are extremely important in the history of cinema.

movies.title: The Homesteader
movies.overview: Directed by Oscar Micheaux and Jerry Mills.

movies.title: The Green Eyed Monster
movies.overview: The Green Eyed Monster is a lost[1] 1919 Black and White silent film action adventure with little to scant information as to its release. It was produced by the Norman Film Manufacturing Company, a historic all-black film production company. Various dates of release are quoted in 1919 and 1921.

movies.title: Within Our Gates
movies.overview: Abandoned by her fiancé, an educated negro woman with a shocking past dedicates herself to helping a near bankrupt school for impoverished negro youths.

movies.title: The Symbol of the Unconquered
movies.overview: Racists learn that the land a negro owns lies over a vast oil field, and threaten his life when he refuses to sell.

movies.title: Body and Soul
movies.overview: A minister is malevolent and sinister behind his righteous facade. He consorts with, and later extorts from, the owner of a gambling house, and betrays an honest girl, eventually driving them both to ruin.

movies.title: The Exile
movies.overview: An idealistic young man is torn between a sultry nightclub owner in Chicago and a Scottish farmgirl in South Dakota.

movies.title: The Emperor Jones
movies.overview: Unscrupulously ambitious, Brutus Jones escapes from jail after killing a guard and through bluff and bravado he finds himself the emperor of a Caribbean island.

movies.title: The Green Pastures
movies.overview: God, heaven, and several Old Testament stories, including the Creation and Noah's Ark, are described supposedly using the perspective of rural, black Americans.

movies.title: Harlem on the Prairie
movies.overview: A cowboy helps a pretty young woman find lost gold.

movies.title: Harlem Rides the Range
movies.overview: A wandering cowboy and his sidekick try to resolve a murder.

movies.title: Lying Lips
movies.overview: A nightclub singer refuses to "date" customers, so she's framed for the murder of her aunt.

movies.title: The Blood of Jesus
movies.overview: Razz accidentally shoots his wife Martha when his hunting rifle drops on the floor and discharges. The church congregation gathers at Martha’s bedside to pray for her recovery, and during this period an angel arrives to take Martha’s spirit from her body, but she is tempted by the slick Judas Green, who is an agent for Satan.

movies.title: Brother Martin: Servant of Jesus
movies.overview: An uncle discusses the life of Martin de Porres with his niece. de Porres was a late sixteenth-century Peruvian who was elevated to sainthood in 1962 by Pope John XXIII.

movies.title: Cabin in the Sky
movies.overview: When compulsive gambler Little Joe Jackson dies in a drunken fight, he awakens in purgatory, where he learns that he will be sent back to Earth for six months to prove that he deserves to be in heaven. He awakens, remembering nothing and struggles to do right by his devout wife, Petunia, while an angel known as the General and the devil's son, Lucifer Jr., fight for his soul.

movies.title: Stormy Weather
movies.overview: Dancing great Bill Williamson sees his face on the cover of Theatre World magazine and reminisces: Just back from World War I, he meets lovely singer Selina Rogers at a soldiers' ball and promises to come back to her when he "gets to be somebody." Years go by, and Bill and Selina's rising careers intersect only briefly, since Selina is unwilling to settle down. Will she ever change her mind? Concludes with a big all-star show hosted by Cab Calloway.

movies.title: Go Down, Death!
movies.overview: The owner of a juke joint arranges to frame an innocent preacher with a scandalous photograph, but his scheme backfires when his own adoptive mother interferes.

movies.title: Dirty Gertie from Harlem U.S.A.
movies.overview: Dirty Gertie is a nightclub entertainer from the Harlem neighborhood of New York City. She arrives on the Caribbean island of "Rinidad" to perform as the headliner in a revue at the Paradise Hotel. On the island she attracts the attention of several men.

movies.title: Boy! What a Girl!
movies.overview: Two silky-smooth producers line up a potential backer (who'll put up half the cash) for a musical review. The catch is that they must find someone else to put up the other half. Enter cigar-smoking cross-dresser "Bumpsie" (Tim Moore), who poses as a wealthy society matron to fool the angel! Features vintage jam sessions with swing drummer Gene Krupa, Big Sid Catlett and his band, The Slam Stewart Trio and The International Jitterbugs.

movies.title: Hi-De-Ho
movies.overview: Cab Calloway plays himself in a plot about jealousy, night clubs, and gangsters. Ends with a series of musical numbers.

movies.title: Sepia Cinderella
movies.overview: A struggling songwriter (Billy Daniels) abandons his girlfriend (Sheila Guyse) for a flashy woman (Tondeleyo) after landing a hit.

information.contentTitle: Race films that stood out at the time
information.contentText: Race films were produced in a wide range of genres: Westerns, musicals, crime dramas, among others. The idea was simple: to give African Americans the opportunity to go and see a film in which they were not portrayed in a stereotyped way.

content_list.content_text: The industry boundaries surrounding race films are complicated and porous, but the filmmakers nonetheless formed a distinct community of practice. Few of these early films survive, so evidence of this community of filmmakers must be drawn from other media: posters, newspaper ads, theater programs and, in some cases, only the handwritten notes of these filmmakers.

information.contentText: Ad for The Homesteader (1919) emphasizing its Black cast

content_list.content_text: The works that scholars generally call "Race films" emerged during the early years of the 20th century. These early films, many of them produced by the Hampton and Tuskegee Institutes, were closely aligned with the African American "uplift" movement and its most prominent exponent, Booker T. Washington (1856-1915). A Trip to Tuskegee (1909), John Henry at Hampton (1913) and A Day at Tuskegee (1913) are all products of that historical moment.

quote.quote: One of the greatest tasks of my life has been to teach the colored man that he can do anything.
quote.author: Oscar Micheaux

content_list.content_text: Alongside the Hampton / Tuskegee films, a group of African American filmmakers and entrepreneurs began to specialize in films made for African American audiences. The Foster Photoplay Company, founded in 1913 by journalist and filmmaker William Foster (1884-1940) — also known as Juli Jones — was one of the first such companies. Foster's own films drew on the uplift movement, telling the story, for example, of a sleeping car attendant: The Railroad Porter (1913), a respected position in the African American community.

Other production companies, such as the Afro-American Film Company, The Hunter C. Haynes Photoplay Company and The Peter P. Jones Photoplay Company, also specialized in films aimed at this audience in the early 1910s. African Americans, like everyone else, were avid moviegoers and, since movie theaters were segregated during this period, there were separate exhibition circuits for African American and white audiences. Some production companies managed to capitalize on this separate circuit by selling films directly to African American theater owners.

content_list.title: Blackface
content_list.description:
Blackface is a practice that is at least 200 years old. It is believed to have begun around 1830 in New York. But it is not just about painting one's skin a different color.

It was a practice in which Black people were ridiculed for the entertainment of white people. Negative stereotypes came attached to the jokes, especially in the United States and Europe. In the 19th century, white actors used paint to blacken their faces in comedic shows, behaving in an exaggerated way to illustrate behaviors that white people associated with Black people. They also mocked the accents of the characters they played. This arose at a time when Black people were not even allowed to take the stage and act because of the color of their skin.

Even in the 20th century, it was very rare for Black actors to be given prominent roles. Roles that called for an African or Asian appearance were often played by white actors in blackface, that is, with their skin darkened. The practice continued on TV shows and in theater for much of the 20th century. The BBC, for example, aired a program that used blackface for 20 years, between 1958 and 1978. The show, called The Black and White Minstrel Show, was extremely popular, with an audience that reached as many as 16 million people. The program won the prestigious Golden Rose of Montreux award in 1961.

As anti-racist movements grew, blackface was gradually eliminated from entertainment and is now seen as shameful and deplorable. But that has not stopped some people from still using the practice.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article O que é 'blackface' e por que é considerado tão ofensivo? (What is 'blackface' and why is it considered so offensive?)

content_list.content_text: The Birth of a Nation (1915), by D. W. Griffith (1875-1948), a film that broke box-office records and drew critical praise, told an extremely racist story, portraying African Americans as rapists and the Ku Klux Klan as a heroic group. Widely protested by African American audiences, The Birth of a Nation prompted a series of cinematic responses — most obviously The Birth of a Race (1918), a famous and troubled production conceived as a direct response to Griffith's film.

Griffith's film helped give a shared (though certainly not unified) purpose to several companies seeking to rehabilitate the image of African Americans on screen, even if profit was something even more important. Among them were the Lincoln Motion Picture Company (founded in 1916) and — the most famous of all the race films companies — the Micheaux Film Corporation, founded in 1918 by author and filmmaker Oscar Micheaux (1884-1951).

information.contentText: One of the few films to catch the attention of the white press, Within Our Gates was lost for more than 70 years and, after being found at the Filmoteca Española, was restored.

content_list.content_text: Oscar Micheaux's films, beginning with The Homesteader (1918), were the most successful race films of their time. Audiences eagerly awaited the release of these films, with their "all-star colored casts," and Within Our Gates (1919) is one of the few examples of a race film that attracted the attention — and an audience — from the white press. While the films of Micheaux and Lincoln found a receptive audience, race films also faced enormous obstacles. Whereas better-funded production companies catering to white audiences could send one film out for distribution while shooting the next, Micheaux and Johnson had to devote their attention and resources to one film at a time.

information.contentText: Some race films released at the time. In order: The Symbol of the Unconquered (1920), Body and Soul (1924), The Blood of Jesus (1914; the first race film added to the United States National Film Registry, in 1991), Harlem on the Prairie (1937; Herb Jeffries in the first western race film) and Carib Gold (1957; considered the last race film ).

content_list.content_text: With the advent of sound, filmmaking became technically more complex and expensive, and companies such as Lincoln, which had always existed on the margins, were increasingly pushed aside. The fact that so few of these films survive is also partly a consequence of these companies' meager finances. The result, combined with consistent underfunding of African American film production, is that many people simply do not know that race films existed. In fact, African American filmmakers have been practicing the craft since the very beginning of the medium.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article Early African American Film – Race Films: History , by Philip Kemp

movies.title: The Birth of a Race
movies.overview: Following the "Birth of the Human Race" section, the film had epic scenes of Ancient Egypt with Nubian soldiers and the rescue of infant Moses in the river. A later scene portrayed Simon of Cyrene helping Jesus carry his cross on the Via Dolorosa and the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The film then shifted to World War I, with two white brothers in a German-American family going to war on the Western Front, one fighting for the United States, and the other fighting for Germany.
